items.question: What is MedLex?
items.answer: A professional education platform for psychiatrists, psychologists, trainees and clinical leaders, founded and led by a UK-trained Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist. It runs three pathways: medico-legal education, examination preparation through The CASC Academy, and professional development through MedLex Foundations.

items.question: Who are the programmes for?
items.answer: Psychiatrists and psychologists who write or may write for courts; MRCPsych CASC candidates and others sitting observed clinical examinations; and clinicians moving into leadership or building a career beyond the clinic. Each pathway states its audience on its own page.

items.question: Which programmes are available now?
items.answer: The CASC Academy is open. Writing Psychiatric Evidence is taking a waitlist for its next cohort. The Foundations programmes are launching; you can register interest and hear when dates are set.

items.question: Are the programmes accredited or CPD-certified?
items.answer: Programmes are independent and are not currently accredited by any college or regulator. Certificates of completion are issued for The CASC Academy. Formal CPD and accreditation are planned as programmes mature and will be stated clearly on each programme page when in place.

items.question: Is MedLex connected to the Royal College of Psychiatrists?
items.answer: No. MedLex is independent and is not endorsed by, affiliated with, or approved by the Royal College. The CASC Academy contains no College examination material; every station is an original, fictional construct.

items.question: Are programmes delivered in English or Arabic?
items.answer: Medico-Legal Education and MedLex Foundations are delivered bilingually in English and Arabic. The CASC Academy is in English only, because the examination is.

items.question: Do I need to be in the UK, Egypt or Qatar?
items.answer: No. Online programmes are open worldwide. Face-to-face elements, where offered, are stated on the programme page with location and dates.

items.question: Does MedLex provide expert opinions or advisory work for institutions?
items.answer: Yes, on a selective basis. Institutional training and advisory work is described on the Institutional page. MedLex does not provide legal advice and does not act for individuals in their own legal matters.

items.question: How do I get in touch?
items.answer: Register your interest for a pathway and you will hear about that pathway only. For institutional enquiries, use the Institutional page. For anything else, the contact page.

paragraphs: MedLex is a founder-led professional education company at the intersection of medicine, law and institutional practice. It exists because the skills that matter most in a clinical career — writing an opinion that survives cross-examination, performing under observation in an examination, leading a service rather than simply running one — are rarely taught in a structured way. Every programme is built by a Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist whose own work spans the clinic, the courtroom, the training programme and the boardroom, and every programme is built to the same standard: a defined question, documented reasoning, and a method the learner can defend afterwards.

Programmes start from the moment the professional will actually face — the question a court has asked, the patient who says something unexpected at minute three, the meeting where a service decision is made — and work backwards to the skill.

Learners leave with work they have done, not notes they have taken: a complete medico-legal report, a station performed under time, a leadership plan for their own service. The output is the evidence of learning.

sampleStation.title: A station, in miniature
sampleStation.subtitle: A shortened taster of how Academy stations work. Full stations unfold over several decision points - this one gives you a single moment, and the examiner's view of it
sampleStation.meta: SAMPLE STATION - SPEAKING WITH A RELATIVE - COMMUNICATION & CONFIDENTIALITY
sampleStation.scenario: Daniel, 24, has been admitted with a first episode of psychosis. He has told the team clearly that he does not want clinical information shared with his family. His mother, distressed, has asked to speak with you. Speak with her
sampleStation.question: She asks you directly: "Just tell me - is it schizophrenia?" What do you do first?

options.text: Reassure her by sharing the likely diagnosis - she is his mother, and she clearly cares about him
options.examinerFeedback: The instinct to comfort is human - and it is exactly where marks leak in this station. Daniel has explicitly declined to share, and disclosing the likely diagnosis breaches that. Strong candidates hold the boundary without abandoning warmth; this option abandons the boundary to keep the warmth

options.text: Explain warmly that you cannot share Daniel's clinical information without his agreement - then explore her concerns, and offer what you can: general information, support for her, and a way forward
options.examinerFeedback: This is what the station is built to reward: the boundary is held, and the relationship is kept. You have declined to disclose, stayed with her distress, and opened a path forward - general information, support, and the possibility of Daniel choosing to involve her. The station rewards doing both at once, not choosing between them

options.text: Tell her that confidentiality rules prevent you discussing anything, and suggest she raises her questions with Daniel himself
options.examinerFeedback: Technically defensible - and it stalls in the communication domain. The task was to manage this conversation, not to end it. Citing the rule and stepping back reads as dismissive, and the marks for engaging with her distress go uncollected

sampleStation.testingTitle: WHAT THIS STATION IS REALLY TESTING
sampleStation.testingBody: Not your knowledge of confidentiality - every candidate knows the rule. It is testing whether you can hold a boundary and a relationship at the same time, under time pressure
sampleStation.disclaimer: This sample uses an original teaching scenario built on the examination's publicly defined competency domains. Select the other options to compare the examiner's view of each

audience.title: A clinical opinion and a legal finding are not the same document
audience.lead: Most psychiatric reports entering court were never written for court. This pathway exists to close that gap — from both ends.
audience.p1: The method is deliberately unglamorous: defined questions, documented reasoning, traceable sources, and conclusions stated at the confidence the evidence supports. That structure is what makes an opinion admissible — and what protects the clinician who signed it.
audience.p2: Nothing is imported wholesale. Programmes are built around the legal frameworks practitioners actually appear under, then aligned with international forensic standards.
audience.quote: “We’re not just training psychiatrists — we’re building the professional standard where clinical expertise becomes court-admissible evidence”

hero.headline: Clinical training makes a doctor. It does not make a career.
hero.lead: Professional development for doctors beyond clinical training: leadership, career, and private practice — the skills every clinician is expected to have, and almost no one is taught.

audience.title: The whole non-clinical side of the job
audience.kicker: Audit, teaching, research, management, your portfolio, the system itself. You are expected to handle all of it from early in your career — and none of it was part of your clinical training.
audience.p1: MedLex Foundations teaches the skills that sit outside clinical knowledge but decide how capable and credible you appear: how your service is actually run, how to communicate so that colleagues listen, how to teach, audit and research with confidence, how to build a portfolio that supports your career, and how to lead a team when the time comes.
audience.p2: Every programme is built by a consultant who has worked inside demanding health systems in the United Kingdom, Egypt and Qatar — and knows exactly where doctors are left to work it out alone.
audience.quote: “If you’ve ever sat in a meeting hoping not to be asked a question, this is for you. You’re not behind — you were just never shown. We’ll show you.”

programmes.title: The Clinician's Edge
programmes.description: 8 modules on the non-clinical skills every doctor is expected to have — from how the system works to preparing for an internal investigation. Short video lessons, interactive pages and a workbook for every module.

programmes.description: What AI can and cannot do in clinical and professional work, how to use it safely and well, and where the professional and medico-legal lines sit.

course.title: 8 modules. 8 skills you will use.
course.lead: One online course covering the whole non-clinical side of the job. Each module explains what you will be expected to do — and what you will be able to do by the end.

modules.title: Understanding How the System Works
modules.description: Roles, hierarchy, rotas, on-call, escalation, and where you sit within it — the UK system as the worked example, with the principles that carry to the Gulf.
modules.small: Walk into any department and understand how it runs.

modules.title: Communication at Work
modules.description: The referral, the email to a consultant, the notes, the handover, the moment you speak up in a meeting — clear, concise, and escalated the right way.
modules.small: Communicate with the clarity colleagues expect of you.

modules.title: Audit & Quality Improvement
modules.description: What audit and QI actually are, how the cycle works from standard to re-audit, the difference between the two, and what you will be asked to do.
modules.small: Take part in audit and QI with real understanding.

modules.title: Research
modules.description: The main types of study and what they are for, what being involved means early on, how to get onto a project, and how to read a paper well enough to discuss it.
modules.small: Hold a conversation about a paper and find a route onto a project.

modules.title: Teaching, Supervision & Feedback
modules.description: Planning and delivering a clear teaching session, supervising juniors, giving feedback that helps — and receiving it well.
modules.small: Teach and supervise in a way that strengthens how you are seen.

modules.title: Management & Leadership Basics
modules.description: How a service is organised, who the key people are, how to work within a team, and the real difference between management and leadership at your level.
modules.small: Step into team and leadership situations with confidence.

modules.title: Portfolio, Appraisal & Revalidation
modules.description: What a portfolio is, what to collect and why, how appraisal works, and how revalidation fits into the longer arc of a career.
modules.small: Know exactly what to collect, from the first day.

modules.title: Preparing for an Internal Investigation
modules.description: The subject no one prepares you for. What an investigation involves, your rights, what to do and avoid early on, and where to find proper support.
modules.small: Understand how investigations work and protect yourself sensibly.

items.a: Fully online and self-paced: short video lessons, interactive pages in each module, and a workbook and toolkit you keep

items.a: Live and face to face, in small cohorts hosted by city. The language — Arabic or English — follows the location

items.q: Is it in English or Arabic?
items.a: The Clinician's Edge is in English. The Clinical Leadership Programme runs in Arabic or English depending on where the cohort is held. Each programme states its language on its own page

items.q: Is the pathway accredited or CPD-certified?
items.a: Programmes are independent and not currently accredited by any college or regulator. You receive a certificate of completion. CPD recognition will be shown on each programme page once it is in place
No. Foundations covers the professional, non-clinical skills of a medical career. It does not teach clinical medicine and does not replace specialty training or local induction

service1.title: Clinical Forensic Assessment
service1.subtitle: Independent psychiatric evaluations built to evidentiary standards
service1.description: We produce court-admissible psychiatric evaluations for civil and criminal cases. Our reports address specific statutory questions with rigorous documentation, diagnostic clarity, and defensible clinical reasoning that withstands cross-examination
features: Criminal responsibility, sanity, and diminished capacity
Fitness to plead and stand trial
Mental capacity, guardianship, and testamentary capacity
Structured violence and recidivism risk assessment (HCR-20 / SAPROF)
Assessment of custodial and prison placement suitability

service2.title: Institutional Policy & Protocols
service2.subtitle: Clinical governance standards that minimise medicolegal risk
service2.description: Healthcare facilities and custodial institutions operate under severe legal scrutiny. We assist leadership in drafting, auditing, and implementing protocols that meet international human rights benchmarks while aligning with local statutory frameworks
features: Involuntary admission & detention compliance frameworks
Seclusion, physical restraint, and de-escalation governance
High-risk incident, suicide, and near-miss investigation protocols
Medicolegal confidentiality, record-keeping, and disclosure policies
Dual-obligation ethics guidance for prison and security-setting clinicians

specCard.clientsValue: Ministries of Health, Hospital Groups, Custodial Services

service3.title: Case Review & Second Opinions
service3.subtitle: Objective forensic audit of complex psychiatric evidence
service3.description: When medical evidence is disputed, contradictory, or methodologically flawed, courts and legal teams require an authoritative, independent second perspective. We provide rigorous review of medical records, existing expert reports, and interview transcripts
features: Evidentiary audit of prior psychiatric expert reports
Identification of cognitive bias, diagnostic overreach, or procedural flaws
Cross-examination briefings and question formulation for trial counsel
Independent expert witness testimony before tribunals and appellate courts
Multidisciplinary case conference facilitation for complex matters

specCard.clientsValue: Judicial Panels, Senior Legal Counsel, Regulatory Bodies

service4.subtitle: Specialised forensic curriculums for judicial and medical personnel
service4.description: We bridge the cultural and intellectual divide between clinical medicine and the law. Our programmes equip judicial officers to critically appraise psychiatric evidence, and teach clinicians how to write reports that survive legal examination
features: Forensic mental health literacy for judges and prosecutors
Accredited medicolegal report writing masterclasses for psychiatrists
Risk formulation and management workshops for clinical teams
Simulated courtroom cross-examination and mock-trial workshops
Continuing Medical / Legal Education (CME/CLE) accredited modules
